implicated_work_descriptions.justification: This is the strongest relationship because the role analyzes user requirements from other national statistical offices and determines appropriate sources of information, methods and approaches. Evidence includes: 'Analyzes the user requirements for data users of other national statistical offices... determines... which sources of information, methods and approaches should be used' and 'Analysis is required to understand and interpret requests for statistical information and to translate them into a concrete, timely and affordable information request.' This aligns most directly with checking data availability and suitability, especially where requests, sources and delivery approaches must be assessed. It is stronger than dissemination subprocesses because the role first determines what information can be provided and by what sources/methods before coordinating delivery. Future drivers such as administrative and alternative data expansion, secure access and enterprise platforms may reshape this work by increasing cross-country source options, data-sharing constraints, and the need to assess feasibility of new data forms and delivery mechanisms.

implicated_work_descriptions.title: Principal Consumer Prices Analyst
implicated_work_descriptions.justification: Check data availability and suitability is the second strongest fit because the role continuously evaluates and researches new data sources, including big data such as 'scanner data' and 'web-scraped data', and determines 'the availability and reliability of new data sources'. It also 'evaluates various data sources for relevance and accuracy when integrating them into the statistical program data'. This is stronger than collection design because the emphasis is on assessing suitability and implications of sources rather than designing instruments or field operations. Future drivers around administrative, alternative and linked data expansion, privacy and secure access, and enterprise platforms will increase source assessment work, especially around nontraditional sources, supplier dependency, quality, legal constraints and production feasibility.

key_activities: Plans and implements long term strategies for the development, enhancement and operation of the highly specialized temporal and spatial consumer price index program. Develops new methods and techniques based on leading edge international developments, to meet the needs of the highly specialized temporal and spatial consumer price index program. Assesses the implications of new approaches and makes recommendations for their adoption.

Performs detailed analysis, evaluation and review of statistical methods and concepts to improve existing data and determines changes in the statistical needs of clients, assessing the impact on the critical programs and developing options and strategies to manage complex issues and multi-stakeholder relations.

Provides expert recommendations, analysis and advice to senior managers in government (from various divisions within Statistics Canada and in key client departments such as Finance Canada and the Bank of Canada) and officials in industry (data providers and users), academia, other national and international statistical institutions and special interest groups.

Oversees and coordinates the review of established statistical methods and processes within the highly specialized realm of temporal and spatial consumer prices indexes. Determines departmental and government-wide impacts and implications and makes recommendations for change.
Implements new systems or methodologies and processes to meet client demands, identifies new statistical methods, techniques and practices and evaluates their cost, efficiency and productivity
Supervision of project teams responsible for statistical outputs, research projects or studies and management of the financial resources attached to each project.

Work is done within the context of temporal and spatial indexes which are used throughout Statistics Canada (i.e., Producer Prices program and the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts), throughout government and industry to index payments worth billions of dollars, and by the Bank of Canada, as the basis for the country’s inflation targeting and monetary policy. Impact of errors is extremely high and cuts across Statistics Canada, other departments and throughout the economy. These factors add to the priority, complexity and scrutiny of the work of this position.

Decision Making: Reviews and evaluates statistical program methods and concepts to improve existing data, to develop new techniques and methods of producing, evaluating and analyzing data and to extend the use and application of departmental statistical programs. Recommendations based on this work have the ability to influence the direction of major corporate initiatives, programs and policies, including those related to big data (e.g., scanner data, web-scraped data).

Initiates changes and implements new systems or methodologies and processes, identifies and assesses new statistical methods, techniques and practices and the associated costs and limitations, identifies the availability and reliability of new data sources, evaluates the suitability of new hardware and software, and identifies and determines the short and long term program impact and benefits. Recommendations lead to changes in approach for the program and take into consideration risks and impacts related to the changes and the use of the resulting program data for indexing and monetary policy purposes.

Manages complex studies related to the temporal and spatial consumer prices program, determines the objectives, content and methodology of such work, defines and sets priorities and milestones, selects and evaluates analytical techniques and methods to be used to integrate and interpret massive volumes of data and organizes the review and presentation of findings. Problems to be resolved usually impact other statistical programs such as Producer Prices and the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts.

Determines objectives and priorities for specific studies and provides expert advice and innovative solutions and recommendations to senior management on course of action and outcomes, or on significant issues affecting temporal and spatial price index programs.
Leadership And Operational Management: Provides advanced subject matter expertise within a multi-disciplinary departmental and interdepartmental project team environment to facilitate big data or temporal and spatial consumer price index research and development activities and establishes objectives and priorities to achieve long term program goals.

Assesses and recommends human and financial resource needs to achieve research and project objectives. Monitors the scope, schedule and cost of the work against approved baselines. Provides input into ongoing and strategic financial planning exercises.

Manages multi-disciplinary intradepartmental and/or interdepartmental project teams involved in research and development activities and establishes objectives and priorities to achieve long term project goals.
For project team members, establishes work objectives and training related to project requirements, monitors achievements and provides input into performance evaluations.
Communication: Provides expert advice and consultative services to senior officials and policy makers at all levels of government, business and national agencies and academics on the results of research and analytical studies, economic and socio-economic theories and principles and statistical concepts and methods as they relate to temporal and spatial consumer price indices.

Attends divisional and intradepartmental meetings and represents the division in interdepartmental and international meetings, conferences and groups to develop consensus or share knowledge in the field of temporal and spatial consumer price indices or big data. Represents, expresses and defends the viewpoint, priorities, conceptual integrity and the validity of methods of the program in venues where decisions are made in order to promote the organization’s interests and influence conceptual directions.

When addressing the general public, explains in clear terms the interpretation of complex data and conceptual frameworks, reasons for variances in the results and the trends derived. When addressing a specialized public, it is also necessary to provide more detailed explanations of the concepts, statistical and analytical approaches used. When media representatives challenge or misinterpret the results of surveys or projects, it is necessary to further explain the results and statistical methods and approaches used in layman’s terms in order to maintain the department's reputation for producing high quality data.
Knowledge of specialized fields: Expert knowledge of economic and sociological principles, concepts and theories, especially as they relate to price index number theory, and specific knowledge of temporal and spatial consumer price indexes. This knowledge is required to provide expert advice on the results of surveys and studies to data users, to STC senior management and to other professionals within and outside STC. It is also required to provide expert evaluation of impacts and risks associated with proposed program changes on the use of the resulting program data for other Statistics Canada programs such as the Producer Prices program and the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts, as well as for government-wide and economy-wide uses such as indexation and monetary policy uses.

Expert knowledge of systems, systems design and practices relevant for the maintenance and development of the temporal and spatial price index statistical programs. *related to the development environment only

Expert knowledge of statistical theories, methods, concepts and practices used in the development, collection, compilation, analysis and interpretation of temporal and spatial price index data in order to develop new methods and techniques and provide expert advice to internal and external stakeholders.
Advanced knowledge of resource and project management practices and principles in order to manage project teams and deliver on high priority projects related to temporal and spatial price indexes.

Advanced knowledge of the methodologies related to the highly specialized fields, such as big data in order to performed detailed analysis and assess new methods relevant to temporal and spatial price indexes.

Knowledge of quantitative analytical methods is required to integrate and interpret massive volumes of data within the context of temporal and spatial price index programs and to provide technical advice to other professionals.
Writing and editing skills to write papers, articles and reports and to determine and assess the design and content of studies, articles and reports that will be disseminated widely or published.
Contextual knowledge: Advanced knowledge of international frameworks (Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts, Prices, etc.), their conceptual building blocks and their interdependencies to contribute in a meaningful way to the evaluation and impact assessment of concepts and compilation methods within the realm of temporal and spatial price indexes.

Knowledge of divisional mandate, policies, priorities, practices, standards and procedures as well as existing databases and conceptual frameworks applicable to the work to incorporate them into the conduct and management of analytical and development projects and to determine or recommend changes.

Knowledge of STC mandate, policies, priorities, practices and classification systems as well as existing data bases, conceptual frameworks, and the statistical methods and procedures applicable to the work, to ensure that they are applied in the conduct of statistical projects and activities, and in the elaboration of recommendations for change to the program.

Research and analysis: Investigates and assesses changes in the statistical needs of clients, determines the extent and approaches of surveys or studies such as the sources of information, statistical techniques, methods and approaches to be used for the collection, processing, analysis and dissemination of price index data. Investigates and challenges existing conceptual frameworks from multiple disciplines and examines multiple variables from distinct sources within the realm of temporal and spatial price indexes to reach new conclusions or generate new solutions. Researches cutting-edge applications of new data sources, including those related to big data to make recommendations on changes to the program. Recommendations made result from work which is evaluated through the lenses of conceptual integrity, operational viability and a deep understanding of the needs of key users for applying the data for indexing and monetary policy purposes.

Interprets the relative quality of data produced, determines reasons for variances, its comparability over time and its relevance in light of changing requirements, trends, developments, policy issues and economic conditions. gsbpm_description: This sub-process documents the findings of the other sub-processes in this phase, in the form of a business case to get approval to implement the new or modified statistical business process. Such a business case would need to conform to the requirements of the approval body, but would typically include elements such as: A description of the “As-Is” business process (if it already exists), with information on how the current statistics are produced, highlighting any inefficiencies and issues to be addressed; The proposed “To-Be” solution, detailing how the statistical business process will be developed to produce the new or revised statistics; An assessment of costs and benefits against objectives and any external constraints. The business case describes options and makes recommendations. It may include the benefits, costs, deliverables, time frame, budget, required technical and human resources, risk assessment and impact on stakeholders for each option. After the business case is prepared, it is submitted for approval to move to the next phase of the business process. At this sub-process, a “go”/“no go” decision is made. Typically, the business case is reviewed and formally approved or disapproved by the appropriate sponsors and governance committees.

5. Contextual knowledge: Knowledge of the departmental and divisional mandate, activities, priorities, practices, standards and procedures applicable to the work to incorporate them into the management of a statistical program and to recommend changes to management.

Knowledge of other statistical programs (concepts, methods, and databases) related to the area of expertise to plan and implement statistical activities, to integrate conceptually different data from other programs, to explain variances and to recommend changes to other statistical programs.

Knowledge of Statistics Canada policies, (e.g. confidentiality of data, security, respondent relations, and data quality), practices and classification systems is required to ensure that they are applied in the conduct of production and dissemination activities.
Knowledge of the policies and programs of key client departments is needed to determine their information requirements.

Knowledge of data users from governments and from the private sector to identify potential new markets, to understand client needs for statistical data or studies, to negotiate contracts and to provide expert advice on program results.

Knowledge of the Statistics Act is needed to explain the legislative requirements to data suppliers/users, and to negotiate special agreements. This knowledge, along with knowledge of the Privacy Act is also required to ensure that the organization meets its commitment to ensuring the confidentiality of all information provided to them and does not release any information that identifies an individual or group without prior consent.
Knowledge of a variety of Acts related to the area of expertise such as the Income Tax Act, the Excise Sales Tax Act, the Employment Insurance Act, and the Corporate Returns Act.
6. Research and analysis: Reviews the conceptual framework of existing statistical programs and determines the need for development, modification and adaption. Programs involve a combination of statistical techniques and methods and the integration of data from a variety of sources (e.g. financial statements, tax files, other administrative sources, surveys, censuses). Source data have often been collected for other purposes using different definitions or concepts and must be translated into common concepts, taking into consideration the impact of the result on other statistical programs as well as departmental priorities.

Assesses new statistical methods, techniques and practices and the associated costs and limitations and identifies the availability and reliability of new data sources to evaluate the suitability of new hardware and software and to determine the short and long term program impact and benefits.

Analyses the relative quality of data produced by statistical programs, determines reasons for variances; reviews the comparability of data over time and relevance in light of trends, developments, changing requirements, policy issues and socio-economic conditions.

Researches gaps and inconsistencies in the production and dissemination methods and procedures, reviews the conceptual framework used and the compatibility with other statistical programs. Problems to be resolved usually impact on other statistical programs.
Investigates client requirements for statistical information and determines the capacity and ability of existing or modified systems to meet these requirements.

implicated_work_descriptions.title: Assistant Director
implicated_work_descriptions.justification: This subprocess is relevant because the role "defends proposals for the development of new surveys," negotiates funding allocation, submits cost estimates, determines broad objectives and project content, and develops recommendations for senior management on new or expanded programs. gsbpm_description: This sub-process prepares a collection strategy for the data, and determines the most appropriate collection instruments and methods, which may depend on the type of data collection, the collection unit type (enterprise, person, or other) and the available sources of data. The actual activities in this sub-process will vary according to the type of collection instrument required, which can include computer assisted interviewing, paper questionnaires, administrative registers, automated and semi-automated data transfer methods (such as using APIs, machine-to-machine integrations and various types of file transfers), web-scraping technologies as well as technology for geospatial data. The collection may employ a multi-mode method which requires additional considerations such as design of sequencing or different instruments for different modes. Direct or indirect use of administrative data may be introduced in the data collection mode for either controlling survey data or assisting it when capturing survey information. In the case of survey (or census) data, this collection strategy includes the design of the collection instruments, questions and response templates (in conjunction with the variables and statistical classifications designed in sub-process 2.2 (Design variables)). It is important to understand respondents and incorporate the user perspectives in the design of data collection. This sub-process may include design of fieldwork operations, and respondent engagement, in the case of survey data collection. It also includes the confirmation of existing agreements or creation of new agreements. This sub-process is enabled by tools such as question libraries (to facilitate the reuse of questions and related attributes), questionnaire tools (to enable the quick and easy compilation of questions into formats suitable for cognitive testing) and agreement templates (to help standardise terms and conditions). This sub-process also includes the design of respondent management systems that are specific to this business process. Where statistical organisations do not collect data directly (i.e. a third party controls the collection and processing of the data), this sub-process may include the design of mechanisms to monitor the data and the metadata to assess impacts of any change made by the third party.

Coordinated execution across collection, processing, analysis and dissemination
workforce_implications: Shift from manual step execution to pipeline supervision
Greater need for workflow configuration and orchestration skills
Greater emphasis on exception handling rather than routine processing
Need for cross-functional coordination across production stages
Increased operational responsibility for monitoring automated end-to-end runs
drivers.impact: Collection design is materially affected because collection methods and interfaces must be designed to feed orchestrated pipelines with standardized, automatable handoffs, metadata capture, and triggerable downstream processing.
impact_mechanisms: Integrated data pipelines require collection inputs to be structured for downstream automated processing
Event-driven workflows depend on collection events, status signals, and machine-readable metadata
Automated handoffs across production stages increase the importance of API-based and machine-to-machine collection patterns
Workforce emphasis shifts from manual collection coordination toward configuring and monitoring collection-to-processing flow

drivers.driver: Metadata-Driven Data Management and Discoverability
drivers.impact: Collection design is materially affected where metadata capture, metadata standards, and metadata exchange with suppliers must be built into collection instruments and transfer arrangements. The driver increases the importance of designing collection so metadata are captured at source and remain usable for discovery and reuse.
impact_mechanisms: Metadata-rich assets require collection instruments and transfer methods to capture structured metadata alongside data.
Standardization pressures collection design toward common templates, question libraries and metadata conventions.
Discoverability and reuse depend on supplier agreements and collection mechanisms that preserve metadata quality and completeness.
Monitoring third-party changes becomes more metadata-centric because metadata are needed to assess downstream interoperability impacts.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning can support smarter routing, respondent management, and collection optimization
